changes.beforeEn: An object grows as it approaches, disappears behind another object, and brightens on its lit surfaces. How does a computer turn all of that into one image? We will follow vertices toward the screen, then connect that journey to the shaders that determine their color.
changes.afterEn: In Townscaper, adding buildings and turning the view changes where roofs appear and how they overlap. How does a computer turn these three-dimensional changes into one image? We will follow vertices toward the screen, connect depth to visibility, and use shaders to calculate surface color. First, let us trace the route from the buildings and camera to the resulting picture.

changes.beforeEn: A depth buffer records which surface is in front at each sample. Consider a convention where smaller values are nearer. If the stored value is 0.7 and a new value is 0.3, the new surface wins and updates color and depth. A later value of 0.8 fails because it is farther away.
changes.afterEn: In Portal, carrying a cube makes it cover parts of the platforms and walls behind it. When several surfaces project onto the same place in the image, the renderer needs a way to decide which surface remains visible. A depth buffer records which surface is in front at each sample. Consider a convention where smaller values are nearer. If the stored value is 0.7 and a new value is 0.3, the new surface wins and updates color and depth. A later value of 0.8 fails because it is farther away.
changes.reason: Observed Portal2007 local445–461 occlusion motivates the depth buffer, not an exposed measured game depth value or early-Z implementation.
